newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia's benchmark bond due early 1997 - Ministry.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia's benchmark bond due early 1997 - Ministry.

text.p: A benchmark Malaysian bond will be issued regularly in small amounts by early next year at the earliest, Finance Ministry Secretary General Clifford Herbert said at the weekend.

The bonds would be issued by the Finance Ministry's holding company, Khazanah Nasional, in amounts of between 100 million and 200 million ringgit each for periods of between five and 10 years, the national news agency Bernama quoted him as saying on Saturday evening.

Malaysian Deputy Prime Minister and Finance Minister Anwar Ibrahim, in the 1997 Malaysian budget unveiled on Friday, proposed a zero-coupon bond issue that would provide a benchmark yield curve for the moribund private debt securities market.
The local bond market has been struggling partly because of the lack of a benchmark to price bond issues, analysts said.
The government was still working on the bonds, which could be used to finance privatised projects, Herbert told a budget seminar organised by the Malaysia Economic Association.

The government, which is expected to show a budget surplus for the fifth straight year in 1997, does not require bonds to raise funds, Herbert said. The new bond was meant only to provide a benchmark for the market, he added.
Anwar announced a one-billion ringgit Savings Bonds issue in the budget. Herbert said these had not been issued in the past because of constraints, but did not elaborate, Bernama said.

Malaysia's bond market was underdeveloped mainly because of a declining supply of tradeable government paper as a result of the Federal Government's budget surpluses and the absence of secondary trading in the domestic bond market, Herbert said.
But he said Malaysia's high investment needs required substantial funding from the financial markets.
The number of government bond issues has also declined because of the privatisation of the large number of state firms and infrastructure projects over the last few years.
Further reforms of the private debt securities market were needed to develop Kuala Lumpur as a regional capital market and service centre in Asia, Herbert said.
